summary: Oregon's first lighthouse was built twice: the first, lit in 1857, was undermined by the river; the second, lit in 1894, still shows a red-and-white first-order Fresnel light.

structures.note: Tower finished August 1892; light first shown 31 December 1894; nomination gives 67 ft

The U.S. Office of Coast Survey in 1849 selected the mouth of the Umpqua River as one of the first sixteen lighthouse locations for the West Coast.
This presented challenges on the south coast along the fifty-five miles from Cape Arago to Heceta Head, which is mainly a dune field lacking rocky promontories.
The chosen spot was Umpqua's low-lying, sandy north spit, roughly equidistant between those headlands.
Hudson's Bay Company operations in the Umpqua Basin, including Fort Umpqua near present-day Elkton, had enhanced the region's economic status.

with initial funds allocated in March 1851. Congress added supplementary appropriations in 1854, and construction began in 1855 with materials delivered from San Francisco.
The first lighthouse was in the Cape Cod style, with keepers' quarters on either side of the 92-foot-tall tower.
The first keeper was Fayette Crosby, a former Scottsburg hotelkeeper.
The light, with its third-order Fresnel lens , was illuminated on October 10, 1857, the first on the Oregon Coast.
An 1861 gale and river flood eroded the lighthouse's foundation, and the building began to tilt.
It was further undermined by a storm in October 1863, and the keepers, with official permission, abandoned the lighthouse in January 1864. The lens was taken out a week later.
While dismantling the lantern room, workers had to flee for their lives when the tower began to totter and then crashed to the ground.
For more than thirty years, there was no lighthouse at the mouth of the Umpqua. The Lighthouse Board simply placed a buoy there. In 1888, Congress finally appropriated money

Coast Guard installed a temporary beacon in the tower and proposed discontinuing use of the Fresnel lens. After local residents protested, the Coast Guard repaired the original mechanism, and the light went back into service in 1985.
The lighthouse and museum are slated to lose Douglas County funding as of July 2018 and are seeking private funding to maintain both facilities.
The lighthouse remains on a U.S. Coast Guard Reservation, adjacent to Umpqua Lighthouse State Park.

resolved_conflicts.explanation: The first tower was lit 10 October 1857 (record events give 1856 or 1857 for 'station established'; work began 1855 or 1856); the present tower was lit 31 December 1894. The record's 1911 first_lit entry is not supported.

The record's 'original lens: order 1' is not supported; Oregon Encyclopedia and Lighthousefriends give a third-order lens for the first tower; the first-order Barbier lens (1890) belongs to the second tower.

notes_for_editor: Sources disagree on: start of work on the first tower (1855 OE, 1856 NRHP/LF), the date of its fall (1863 NRHP, Jan-Feb 1864 OE/LF), tower height (67 ft NRHP, 65 ft LF), and the record's agency (record says Douglas County Museum Foundation; sources say Douglas County; OE says county funding was to end July 2018, current operator unverified). Tour hours and whether the tower is climbable now are from Lighthousefriends and should be rechecked. Light-House Board OCR prints 1802 for 1892 (metalwork, tower completion); read as 1892 from context and the 1893 report. Printed page numbers of the 1891/1892 volume were not confirmed so scan pages are cited. No 1860s Board reports were in the corpus, so the 1861-64 account rests on the Oregon Encyclopedia and Lighthousefriends; Marinus Stream's drowning (about 1896) rests on Lighthousefriends alone. The 1909 piracy story rests on the nomination citing Jim Gibbs and was not independently verified; the ship is probably the steamer Beckman (nomination OCR 'BCJCKMAN') but no source read says so. Roster stints are from the USLHS archive; none were matched by name to other stations. Quotation of the Chronicling America pages found nothing relevant.
